newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's truth body says police want to tell all.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's truth body says police want to tell all.

text.p: Five former secret policemen have stepped forward to tell all about dozens of killings of black activists in the apartheid years, South Africa's "truth commission" on human rights abuses said on Saturday.
The five, including a former police brigadier who ran a notorious death-squad unit, want amnesty for their crimes in return.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu's statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission, set up to probe atrocities in the battle over white domination, has so far mainly heard testimony from blacks who suffered, but few perpetrators have come clean in return for forgiveness.

Brigadier Jack Cronje, a former commander of a secret police unit at Vlakplaas near Pretoria in the 1980s, is among the five wanting amnesty "for incidents involving about 40 deaths", the commission said in a statement.

The men, who are to submit their applications on Monday, want to come clean on several high-profile killings, including the fate of three black community leaders from the Eastern Cape province who vanished in 1985.

"Bombings, petrol bombings, weapons smuggling and the supply of booby-trapped hand grenades are among other activities which we expect to be dealt with in the amnesty application," the commission said.

The five policemen are also expected to give details of the death of Fabian Ribeiro, an activist of Nelson Mandela's then-banned African National Congress, who was murdered in 1986. His family went to court unsuccessfully earlier this year in an effort to prevent the truth commission from granting pardons.
A commission official declined to give further details of the acts of violence, saying these would come out when the five appear before the truth commission's amnesty committee from October 21.

The announcement came a day after former defence minister Magnus Malan was acquitted in South Africa's supreme court of masterminding the massacre of 13 blacks by a death squad in 1987. The court found there was no evidence to link him and over a dozen other former soldiers and policemen to the killings.
One apartheid policeman who has been found guilty of atrocities is former colonel Eugene de Kock, convicted of six murders and a string of lesser crimes committed while he headed the Vlakplaas unit.
He has pointed fingers in many directions, including at apartheid-era presidents who he said were involved in the "dirty war" against black activists fighting to end centuries of white domination.

De Kock, who claims to be apartheid's most successful assassin, was known to his colleagues as "Prime Evil" and his court testimony has exposed more details about crimes in defence of apartheid than Tutu's commission.
Critics say it has had little success so far in exposing the truth of human rights abuses in the final 30 years of apartheid.

The body, which has the power to subpoena witnesses and grant amnesty to criminals and compensation to those who suffered, has been showing signs of frustration at the reluctance of the guilty to trade confessions for pardons.
It has started wielding the stick to force former law and order minister Adriaan Vlok and eight retired police chiefs and generals to appear for questioning.
